title: kirtan repertoire (20 songs)
hook: a refrain that never changes, and a list that slips in hunger, sleep and error beside peace and compassion

segments.voice: Yesterday, kirtan repertoire: Govinda jaya jaya, Krishna's names sung like a call: the names are already doing the calling. Whose name did you say with full attention? Day nine hundred ninety-one.
screen: `KIRTAN REPERTOIRE.` · `GOVINDA JAYA JAYA, NAMES AS A CALL.`

segments.voice: Halfway through the evening, the music changes key and the room turns toward the Goddess. The leader begins a verse that has the same ending every time, a run of bows that the whole room picks up almost at once. Only one word in the middle changes. Peace. Faith. Compassion. Mother. Words that sound right for a hymn to a goddess. But if you stay for the whole list, other words come round too, words nobody would put on a greeting card. Hunger. Sleep. Thirst. And, near the end, error.
screen: `THE ROOM TURNS TO THE GODDESS.` → `ONE WORD CHANGES EACH TIME.` → `PEACE, FAITH ... HUNGER, ERROR.`

segments.voice: The song comes from the Devi Mahatmya, the Glory of the Goddess, a text set inside the Markandeya Purana. In its fifth chapter the gods, driven from heaven, go to the Himalaya and praise her. The verse they repeat goes like this in Sanskrit: ya devi sarva-bhuteshu, and then a quality, rupena samsthita, namas tasyai, namas tasyai, namas tasyai, namo namah. In paraphrase: to the Goddess who dwells in all beings in the form of this, bow to her, bow to her, bow to her, bow, bow. Then the gods fill in the blank, verse after verse. Consciousness. Intelligence. Sleep. Hunger. Shadow. Power. Thirst. Patience. Modesty. Peace. Faith. Loveliness. Fortune. Memory. Compassion. Contentment. Mother. And error, the word bhranti, confusion, mistaking one thing for another. So the hymn doesn't only find her in the parts of life that look holy. It finds her in the tired body asking for sleep, the stomach asking for food, even the mind that gets things wrong. For Shaktas, Hindus who honor the Goddess as the highest, this is close to the heart of the matter: she is the power moving through everything, the plain and the bright alike. Sung as kirtan, the structure does something lovely. The bow at the end never changes, so even someone who doesn't know Sanskrit can join it from the second verse. The changing word is the leader's job. The room's job is to keep bowing, whatever word comes up. Hunger, bow. Error, bow.
screen: `FROM THE DEVI MAHATMYA.` · `TO THE GODDESS IN ALL BEINGS.` · `IN SLEEP, HUNGER, EVEN ERROR.` · `THE BOW NEVER CHANGES.` · then, large: `WHATEVER COMES UP, BOW.`

segments.voice: Check in with the body, from the stomach up. Is there hunger, tiredness, thirst, restlessness? Name whatever is here, plainly, one word at a time. Then name something brighter that's also here: a little patience, a memory, some contentment. Don't rank them. Let each word come and go like the changing word in the hymn. If you pray, you can follow each word with the hymn's refrain, said silently. If not, simply notice that both kinds of word belong to the same life. The bell holds the time.
Kirtan repertoire. Today's song: ya devi sarva-bhuteshu, to the Goddess in all beings, found in peace and compassion, and in hunger, sleep and error too.
Your line: Hunger, bow. Error, bow. Today, the next time you catch yourself in a mistake, name it plainly once, the way the hymn names error, before any scolding starts. Day nine hundred ninety-one.

howItsDone: The ya devi sarva-bhuteshu verses are recited and sung in Goddess worship, especially during Navaratri, and at kirtans the room often joins the unchanging bow while a leader sings the changing word.

fork.setup: you're one of the gods praising the Goddess in all beings. you've named peace, faith and compassion. does 'error' go on the list?
options: yes. she dwells in error too.
only if it's someone else's error.
fork.reveal: the Devi Mahatmya names bhranti, error, among the forms in which she dwells in all beings, alongside hunger, sleep and thirst.

original.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: namas tasyai, bow to her. The unchanging bow that ends each verse.

trapdoor: what you thought: a hymn to a goddess praises only beautiful things.
what it means: this hymn bows to the Goddess in all beings, in hunger, sleep and error as well as peace and compassion.
what a scholar hears: Devi Mahatmya chapter five, the gods' praise, set inside the Markandeya Purana.
